title: Scientific Opinion on the re-evaluation of ascorbic acid (E 300), sodium ascorbate (E 301) and calcium ascorbate (E 302) as food additives
authors: EFSA Panel on Food Additives and Nutrient Sources added to Food (ANS)
funder: European Food Safety Authority, on request from the European Commission (Question Nos EFSA-Q-2011-00470, EFSA-Q-2011-00471 and EFSA-Q-2011-00472), adopted on 14 April 2015. Use levels were provided by FoodDrinkEurope, ICGA, FCRA, Specialised Nutrition Europe, OIV and UNESDA; unpublished toxicity reports were submitted by DSM.
authorConflicts: Declarations of interest of panel members are held by EFSA; not read.
result: E 300 (INS 300) is identical to L-ascorbic acid, C6H8O6, 176.12 g/mol. Absorption by sodium-dependent active transport is up to 98% at low doses, 80-90% up to 180 mg, 75% at 1 g and 16% at 12 g; above 80-100 mg/day most further absorbed ascorbate is excreted unchanged in urine. Dehydroascorbic acid can be reduced back to ascorbic acid or irreversibly hydrolysed to diketogulonic acid, oxidised mainly to oxalic and L-threonic acid. Sodium and calcium ascorbate dissociate fully in the stomach. In the presence of copper(II) or iron(III), small amounts of benzene can form from benzoic acid; German non-alcoholic beverages measured in 2010 contained less than the EU drinking-water limit of 1 ug/L. Pro-oxidant and mutagenic effects with redox-active metal ions in some in vitro systems have not been confirmed in vivo. No adverse effects in animal studies at the highest doses tested; bladder tumour promotion by 5% dietary sodium ascorbate in initiated male rats was attributed to sodium. Epidemiology indicated that vitamin C below 1500 mg/day is not a risk factor for kidney stones, although the cited cohort of Taylor et al. (2004) reported a relative risk of 1.41 (95% CI 1.11 to 1.80) in men at 1000 mg/day or more. JECFA allocated a group ADI 'not specified' in 1981; the Panel saw no need for a numerical ADI. In the EU, E 300-302 belong to Group I and are authorised at quantum satis in most foods, with 200 or 300 mg/kg in processed cereal-based foods and baby foods (FCS 13.1.3). In bread, industry reported its function as a flour treatment agent. Fine bakery wares, unprocessed fruit and vegetables, fruit juices and flavoured drinks were the main contributors to additive exposure.
